screens.title: Error Handling and Gas Optimization Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a practical mental model for when to use require, revert, and assert, and why custom errors and careful data choices save gas. We'll connect error semantics to gas effects: require and revert signal external checks and refund remaining gas, assert flags internal invariants and consumes remaining gas. You will also learn the three primary storage locations—storage, memory, calldata—and the optimization patterns that follow from them. Examples include replacing expensive string messages with custom errors, packing small variables into a single slot, preferring events for off-chain logs, and designing loops to avoid costly storage reads. These ideas matter because gas directly affects user adoption and security: misused assertions or frequent storage writes can cause high fees or hide bugs. As we progress you will examine a compact Wallet contract that demonstrates custom errors, variable packing, calldata use, and how deposits and withdrawals behave under failure. Keep an eye on simple contrasts — external vs internal checks, persistent vs temporary data — so you can make concrete trade-offs when writing or reviewing contracts. By the end you'll have clear rules and examples to apply immediately to your code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will clearly differentiate require, revert, and assert and choose the appropriate one for each situation. You will be able to implement custom errors to produce descriptive, gas-efficient revert data and decode why they are cheaper than strings. You will understand storage, memory, and calldata differences, and pick the most efficient data location for arguments and temporary values. Finally, you will apply concrete gas-optimization patterns: minimize writes to storage, pack state variables to reduce slots, prefer events for off-chain logs, use short-circuiting and bounded loops, and mark functions view or pure when appropriate. Each objective includes a practical reason: choosing the right error behavior prevents unintended state changes or hidden bugs; custom errors reduce transaction cost and make frontends easier to decode; selecting the right data location directly lowers per-call gas; and the collection of gas patterns reduces fees for users and keeps DApps competitive. You will practice these skills with a compact Wallet contract that demonstrates deposits, withdrawals, a custom error, variable packing, and calldata usage so you can compare gas numbers in a real example.

screens.title: require(), revert(), and assert() — Roles and Gas Differences
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity offers three core ways to stop execution and revert state: require, revert, and assert. Each has a distinct role. Use require to validate inputs and external conditions such as access control or argument validity. When a require fails it reverts and refunds the remaining gas, and often includes a string message to help the caller. revert is a direct statement you can use inside conditional logic where multi-step checks are clearer written as if statements; it behaves like require in gas refunding and reversion. assert is reserved for invariants that should never break. If an assert fails, it indicates a bug or corrupted state and consumes all remaining gas, making failures loud and signaling a serious issue. A common misconception is using assert for input validation—doing so risks losing the refund behavior and hides the possibility that the error was due to user input. Concrete example: require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function") is correct for access checks; assert(tokenSupply == computedSupply) is appropriate for internal consistency after a complex operation. Remember that require and revert refund remaining gas but still consume gas up to the failure point; assert consumes the rest as well. When deciding, ask: can this condition be false because of user input or state visible to an external caller? If yes, prefer require or revert. Is it an invariant that only internal logic can break? Then assert is the right tool. This decision affects both safety and cost for users.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Error primitives
Comparison table
require()
Validate external conditions and user input. Reverts and refunds remaining gas. Can include a string message for clarity.
revert()
Use inside conditional logic or complex checks. Equivalent refund behavior to require but written as a statement.
assert()
For invariants that should never fail. Consumes remaining gas when triggered and signals critical bugs.
Concrete example
Use require for access checks like require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function"). Use revert when you need an if block, for example: if (balance < amount) { revert("Insufficient balance"); }. Use assert for invariants such as assert(totalSupply == internalSum) after a transfer.
Common mistake
Using assert for input validation. That can needlessly consume all gas and misclassify normal failures as bugs.
Pro tip
If a condition can fail due to user data, prefer require or revert and consider a custom error instead of a long string.
Key Takeaway

Match the primitive to the failure type: external vs internal. This choice affects both safety and gas outcomes.

screens.title: Custom Errors — Why and How
screens.narratorSegment: Custom errors were introduced to let developers return structured, compact error data instead of long dynamic strings. Define an error type once, for example: error InsufficientBalance(uint256 available, uint256 required); and then revert with revert InsufficientBalance(balance, amount);. This approach stores the error selector and the typed arguments, which is far smaller on-chain than a string message. Use custom errors when you want to report values back to the caller while minimizing gas. They also make it easier for frontends and block explorers to decode failure reasons without parsing strings. A practical pattern is to define a set of domain-specific errors at the top of your contract and use them consistently across functions. Remember not to hide sensitive internal state in error arguments; error data is visible in transaction traces. A common misconception is that custom errors are only about readability; their primary advantage is gas savings because strings are dynamic and more expensive to encode. In the Wallet example you will see InsufficientFunds(balance, amount) used to report available and requested quantities. When refactoring a string revert into a custom error, measure gas with a profiler to confirm the improvement. A closing question: which frequent revert messages in your codebase could be converted to typed errors for both clarity and cost reduction?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Custom Errors
What a custom error looks like
error InsufficientFunds(uint256 available, uint256 requested);

// Usage:
if (balance < amount) { revert InsufficientFunds(balance, amount); }
Custom errors pack a selector and typed arguments. They are especially useful when you need to return numeric context alongside the failure reason.
When to use
Replace long string messages used in require or revert with typed errors when you want to save gas and provide structured data.
Example
In GasOptimizedWallet: revert InsufficientFunds(balance, _amount); returns both values so the UI can display them precisely.
Misconception
Custom errors are not only for clarity; they are primarily a gas optimization over strings.

screens.title: Storage, Memory, and Calldata
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity has three primary data locations you will use frequently: storage, memory, and calldata. storage persists on-chain and is the most expensive to write; every SSTORE and SLOAD has a real gas cost. Use storage only for true persistent state. memory is temporary and exists for the scope of a function call; it is cheaper than storage and useful for local copies and return buffers. calldata is immutable data provided by external function calls. For external functions that accept large arrays or byte buffers but do not modify them, calldata is the cheapest and avoids copying into memory. A common rule: for external function parameters that you will not mutate, declare them as calldata to avoid needless copying. For example, a function that accepts bytes calldata data returns data. length without copying it into memory. Also note that reading from storage inside tight loops is costly; prefer copying a storage reference into memory when you will access it multiple times in a function. A common misconception is that memory is free—it is not, but it is substantially cheaper than storage for temporary operations. Always ask: does this value need to be stored across transactions? If yes, use storage. If the value is transient or an external input that won’t be modified, favor memory or calldata respectively to reduce gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Data locations
Quick reference
storage
Persistent state stored on-chain. Writes are expensive. Use only for data you must keep between transactions.
memory
Temporary data for the life of the call. Cheaper than storage and good for local computation.
calldata
Immutable function parameters for external calls; cheapest for large inputs that won’t be modified.
Concrete guidance
  • Use calldata for external bytes or arrays you don't modify to avoid copying into memory.
  • Copy storage values into memory when reading them multiple times to reduce repeated SLOADs.
  • Reserve storage writes for necessary persistent updates only.
Example
function processLargeData(bytes calldata _data) public pure returns (uint256) { return _data.length; } — calldata avoids copying the full bytes array into memory.
Key Takeaway

Pick calldata for unmodified external inputs, memory for temporary work, and storage only for persisted state to control gas cost.

screens.title: Minimize Storage Writes & Use Events for Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Storage writes are the single most expensive operations you will perform on-chain. Designing your contract to minimize SSTORE calls reduces deployment and per-call costs. Start by asking whether a value truly needs to persist. If it is only necessary for off-chain UIs or analytics, emit an event instead of writing to storage. Events are significantly cheaper than SSTORE and enable efficient retrieval by indexers. When you must update storage, try to batch updates or avoid toggling a storage slot repeatedly. Another pattern is to keep frequently changing counters in smaller packed slots or update derived values off-chain. Also be mindful of initializations: writing a zero to a slot that was already zero still consumes gas, so set defaults carefully. Best practice includes copying storage into memory for multiple reads inside a function and writing back only once if needed. For loops that update storage, consider accumulating results in memory and performing a single storage write at the end. A common mistake is treating events as ephemeral and storing the same data anyway. If the contract doesn't need to read the data on-chain later, prefer events for logging actions like deposits or user actions. Finally, marking read-only helpers view or pure allows callers to simulate behavior off-chain without a transaction cost.

keyIdea.text: Avoid frequent SSTOREs by using events for logs, batching writes, and using memory for intermediate computation to lower gas usage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Storage & Events
Process checklist to minimize storage cost
  1. Decide if a value must persist on-chain. If not, emit an event.
  2. Batch or consolidate updates to avoid multiple SSTOREs.
  3. Use memory for repeated reads and write back to storage only once.
  4. Prefer smaller types and packing to reduce slot count for frequent updates.
Example
Emit Deposit and Withdrawal events for UI updates rather than storing each action in an on-chain array when not required for contract logic.
Common mistake
Writing every user action to storage for convenience. That multiplies SSTORE costs and often could be replaced by cheaper events.
Key Takeaway

Prefer events for off-chain logs and limit SSTORE to essential persistent state; copy to memory for heavy reads and write back sparingly.

screens.title: Loop Efficiency and Short-Circuiting
screens.narratorSegment: Loops can be attractive but expensive when they repeatedly access storage or iterate over unbounded arrays. A loop that touches storage on every iteration multiplies SLOAD and SSTORE costs. Prefer designs that keep arrays small and bounded, or offload full scans to off-chain indexers. For on-chain processing, use pagination patterns so each transaction does a limited chunk of work. When iterating, copy frequently used storage values into memory once and reuse the in-memory copy to avoid multiple SLOADs. Short-circuiting with logical operators is another inexpensive gas control: expressions using && and || evaluate left to right and stop as soon as the outcome is determined. For example, require(condition1 && expensiveCheck(), "Error") will avoid calling expensiveCheck when condition1 is false. A common mistake is writing require with multiple expensive calls that always run; instead, reorder conditions so cheap checks run first. Also be careful with unbounded for loops across user-controlled collections. Concrete pattern: if you need to remove multiple elements, consider a mapping-based approach or mark items inactive and prune off-chain. The core rule: bound work performed in a single transaction and favor memory copies and short-circuit ordering to minimize repeated or unnecessary gas usage.

keyIdea.title: Loop safety rule
keyIdea.text: Bound loop work, copy storage into memory for repeated reads, and order boolean checks so cheap conditions short-circuit expensive ones.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Loop & Short-circuit
Loop optimization checklist
  1. Limit iterations per transaction with pagination or bounded loops.
  2. Copy storage values into memory if accessed repeatedly inside the loop.
  3. Avoid loops over large dynamic arrays stored on-chain; prefer mappings and indices.
Short-circuit tip
Order boolean conditions so cheap checks run first. This prevents expensive function calls when earlier checks already determine the result.
Misconception
Assuming a single loop over a large array is OK. On-chain iteration multiplies storage cost and can run out of gas.
Key Takeaway

Design for bounded work, use memory caches for repeated reads, and leverage short-circuiting to skip expensive checks when possible.

screens.title: Variable Packing and Slot Layout
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity packs state variables into 256-bit storage slots where possible. By grouping smaller variables such as uint8, uint64, and bool together, you can place multiple values in a single slot and reduce the number of SSTORE operations required. The lesson provides a concrete struct example: UserData with uint256 id; uint128 lastLogin; bool isAdmin; uint64 reputation; initially this layout typically uses multiple slots because of the large uint256. Reordering fields so the smaller ones are grouped together and the large uint256 sits separately helps the compiler pack them more efficiently. For instance, placing uint64 reputation, uint128 lastLogin, bool isAdmin together allows them to fit within a single 256-bit slot, and keeping uint256 id in its own slot. A common misconception is that ordering doesn't matter; in practice the compiler packs contiguous smaller fields into the same slot if their combined width fits within 256 bits. When optimizing, weigh readability and future changes against packing gains: adding another large variable may break a packing strategy and increase slots. Always test with the compiler and examine the storage layout to confirm the expected packing. The payoff comes when writing or updating these fields: fewer slots mean fewer SSTOREs and lower gas for state changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Variable Packing
Packing illustration
Original struct might spread values across more slots. Reordering groups smaller types into one slot and places large types in separate slots.
// Original
struct UserData {
  uint256 id;
  uint128 lastLogin;
  bool isAdmin;
  uint64 reputation;
}

// Optimized ordering
struct UserData {
  uint64 reputation;
  uint128 lastLogin;
  bool isAdmin;
  uint256 id;
}
Why it saves gas
Fewer storage slots means fewer SSTORE operations when updating packed fields, lowering transaction gas.
Caveat
Packing can be fragile if you later add large types. Re-check compiler layout after changes.
Key Takeaway

Reorder fields to group smaller types. Always validate the compiled storage layout to confirm slot usage.

screens.title: GasOptimizedWallet — Structure and Intent
screens.narratorSegment: We'll step through the GasOptimizedWallet contract to link the theory to a real example. The contract defines a custom error InsufficientFunds to report available and requested amounts when a withdraw fails, saving gas compared to string messages. It demonstrates variable packing with balance stored as uint128, lastWithdrawalTime as uint64, and a bool isActive; these smaller types are chosen to fit into single 256-bit slots where possible and reduce SSTORE costs when updated. The deposit function uses require to validate that the wallet is active and the deposit amount is positive, then updates the packed balance and emits a Deposit event for off-chain UIs. The withdraw function uses the onlyOwner modifier, checks activity with require, and reverts with the custom error when the balance is insufficient. It then updates packed variables and triggers a transfer and a Withdrawal event. The contract also includes processLargeData with bytes calldata to show that calldata avoids copying input data into memory if it is not modified. Walkthrough tip: when you test this contract, observe the Withdrawal event and the encoded InsufficientFunds error on failure to see both the human-readable reason and the compact revert data. This contract ties together many optimizations we've discussed in a small, auditable example.

narration.text: We'll step through the GasOptimizedWallet contract to link the theory to a real example. The contract defines a custom error InsufficientFunds to report available and requested amounts when a withdraw fails, saving gas compared to string messages. It demonstrates variable packing with balance stored as uint128, lastWithdrawalTime as uint64, and a bool isActive; these smaller types are chosen to fit into single 256-bit slots where possible and reduce SSTORE costs when updated. The deposit function uses require to validate that the wallet is active and the deposit amount is positive, then updates the packed balance and emits a Deposit event for off-chain UIs. The withdraw function uses the onlyOwner modifier, checks activity with require, and reverts with the custom error when the balance is insufficient. It then updates packed variables and triggers a transfer and a Withdrawal event. The contract also includes processLargeData with bytes calldata to show that calldata avoids copying input data into memory if it is not modified. Walkthrough tip: when you test this contract, observe the Withdrawal event and the encoded InsufficientFunds error on failure to see both the human-readable reason and the compact revert data. This contract ties together many optimizations we've discussed in a small, auditable example.

keyIdea.title: Practical demo
keyIdea.text: The GasOptimizedWallet encapsulates custom errors, variable packing, calldata use, and event-based logging to illustrate gas-conscious patterns.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › GasOptimizedWallet Walkthrough
Key contract excerpts
// error InsufficientFunds(uint256 available, uint256 requested);

address public owner;
uint128 public balance;
uint64 public lastWithdrawalTime;
bool public isActive;

event Deposit(address indexed user, uint256 amount);
event Withdrawal(address indexed user, uint256 amount);

function deposit() public payable {
  require(isActive, "GO_Wallet: Wallet is inactive");
  require(msg.value > 0, "GO_Wallet: Deposit amount must be greater than zero");
  balance += uint128(msg.value);
  emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value);
}

function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public onlyOwner {
  require(isActive, "GO_Wallet: Wallet is inactive");
  if (balance < _amount) { revert InsufficientFunds(balance, _amount); }
  balance -= uint128(_amount);
  lastWithdrawalTime = uint64(block.timestamp);
  payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);
  emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, _amount);
}
Highlights
Custom error replaces strings on withdraw failure. Packed state variables reduce slot usage. Events signal off-chain clients.
Calldata demo
processLargeData(bytes calldata _data) returns _data.length to show calldata avoids copying for readonly arrays.
Key Takeaway

Small, deliberate choices—custom errors, packing, calldata, events—compound to lower gas and improve UX in live contracts.

screens.title: String Messages vs Custom Errors — Gas Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: String messages in require or revert are simple to read but expensive because strings are dynamic types that need length encoding and storage in calldata or memory. Every character increases the encoded size and thus the gas required to include that message in a revert. Custom errors, by contrast, include a fixed selector and typed arguments that are narrower to encode. The trade-off is clarity versus cost: a long user-facing string can be helpful during development, but in production it often makes sense to convert repeated or widely used messages into custom errors to reduce gas. A practical refactor path is to identify frequent revert strings—access control, balance checks—and replace them with well-named custom errors. For example, change require(balance >= amount, "Insufficient funds") to if (balance < amount) { revert InsufficientFunds(balance, amount); }. When you perform this refactor, run a gas profiler to compare the two flows: the custom error should show lower gas usage on failure and often on successful paths as well because the compiler can optimize dynamic string usage. Keep in mind error decoding on the frontend: custom errors need decoding logic or support in tooling, but they enable precise, typed information for better UI messages.

screens.title: Events vs Storage for Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Events provide a cost-efficient way to record contract activity for off-chain consumption. Unlike storage, events are not accessible to contract code for logic, but they are indexed and easily read by clients and block explorers. When you need a trace of actions for UI updates or analytics, emit an event rather than storing structured logs in a state variable. Events are logged in transaction receipts and indexed topics, letting indexers reconstruct timelines without expensive SSTOREs. A common mistake is duplicating data: both emitting an event and storing the same data in state. If the contract logic does not later require those stored values, remove the storage write and rely on events. Keep event payloads to the essential fields you need off-chain—reducing event size also reduces gas. Example: emit Deposit(address indexed user, uint256 amount) provides the UI with everything it needs to show a deposit without writing the amount to a storage array. Finally, use events thoughtfully for auditability and transparency, but do not treat them as a substitute when contract logic must query the historical data on-chain; events are for off-chain workflows, storage is for on-chain logic.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Events vs Storage
Decision guide
  • If data is only needed by UIs or analytics, emit an event.
  • If contract logic must read the historical data later, persist it in storage.
  • Keep event payloads minimal to lower gas and indexer load.
Example
Use Deposit and Withdrawal events for UI updates instead of appending every action to an on-chain array.
Watchout
Events are not readable by contracts. Do not rely on them for on-chain state or access control decisions.
Key Takeaway

Prefer events for off-chain logging and UIs; keep storage for data the contract must use on-chain.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, require and revert are for external checks and refund remaining gas, while assert signals internal invariants and consumes remaining gas. Second, custom errors are the preferred production pattern to report typed failure data while saving gas compared to string messages. Third, choose data locations deliberately: storage is persistent and expensive, memory is temporary for call-time work, and calldata is the cheapest for immutable external inputs. Each of these choices impacts safety, clarity, and transaction cost. Keep these principles in mind when writing or auditing contracts: match error primitives to failure types, prefer custom errors for frequent or data-rich reverts, and minimize persistent writes. These core rules will guide you to safer and more economical smart contracts. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a practical mental model for when to use require, revert, and assert, and why custom errors and careful data choices save gas. We'll connect error semantics to gas effects: require and revert signal external checks and refund remaining gas, assert flags internal invariants and consumes remaining gas. You will also learn the three primary storage locations—storage, memory, calldata—and the optimization patterns that follow from them. Examples include replacing expensive string messages with custom errors, packing small variables into a single slot, preferring events for off-chain logs, and designing loops to avoid costly storage reads. These ideas matter because gas directly affects user adoption and security: misused assertions or frequent storage writes can cause high fees or hide bugs. As we progress you will examine a compact Wallet contract that demonstrates custom errors, variable packing, calldata use, and how deposits and withdrawals behave under failure. Keep an eye on simple contrasts — external vs internal checks, persistent vs temporary data — so you can make concrete trade-offs when writing or reviewing contracts. By the end you'll have clear rules and examples to apply immediately to your code.

By the end of this chapter you will clearly differentiate require, revert, and assert and choose the appropriate one for each situation. You will be able to implement custom errors to produce descriptive, gas-efficient revert data and decode why they are cheaper than strings. You will understand storage, memory, and calldata differences, and pick the most efficient data location for arguments and temporary values. Finally, you will apply concrete gas-optimization patterns: minimize writes to storage, pack state variables to reduce slots, prefer events for off-chain logs, use short-circuiting and bounded loops, and mark functions view or pure when appropriate. Each objective includes a practical reason: choosing the right error behavior prevents unintended state changes or hidden bugs; custom errors reduce transaction cost and make frontends easier to decode; selecting the right data location directly lowers per-call gas; and the collection of gas patterns reduces fees for users and keeps DApps competitive. You will practice these skills with a compact Wallet contract that demonstrates deposits, withdrawals, a custom error, variable packing, and calldata usage so you can compare gas numbers in a real example.

Beyond understanding, you'll demonstrate practical skills by deploying a small contract, exercising both successful and failing flows, and inspecting the revert data. You will write and trigger a custom error and observe how the encoded arguments allow your frontend to present precise failure messages. You will also design a small refactor that replaces a costly string revert with a custom error, then run a quick gas comparison to see the savings. For storage and packing, you'll reorder fields in a struct, reason about how many storage slots remain, and explain why the new layout uses fewer SSTORE operations on updates. Finally you will produce short notes that justify whether to use events or storage for a particular piece of information, and mark functions pure or view where appropriate for off-chain callers. These artifacts — contract deployment, event logs, gas numbers, and refactor notes — serve as verifiable milestones showing you applied the concepts, not just memorized them.

Solidity offers three core ways to stop execution and revert state: require, revert, and assert. Each has a distinct role. Use require to validate inputs and external conditions such as access control or argument validity. When a require fails it reverts and refunds the remaining gas, and often includes a string message to help the caller. revert is a direct statement you can use inside conditional logic where multi-step checks are clearer written as if statements; it behaves like require in gas refunding and reversion. assert is reserved for invariants that should never break. If an assert fails, it indicates a bug or corrupted state and consumes all remaining gas, making failures loud and signaling a serious issue. A common misconception is using assert for input validation—doing so risks losing the refund behavior and hides the possibility that the error was due to user input. Concrete example: require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function") is correct for access checks; assert(tokenSupply == computedSupply) is appropriate for internal consistency after a complex operation. Remember that require and revert refund remaining gas but still consume gas up to the failure point; assert consumes the rest as well. When deciding, ask: can this condition be false because of user input or state visible to an external caller? If yes, prefer require or revert. Is it an invariant that only internal logic can break? Then assert is the right tool. This decision affects both safety and cost for users.

Custom errors were introduced to let developers return structured, compact error data instead of long dynamic strings. Define an error type once, for example: error InsufficientBalance(uint256 available, uint256 required); and then revert with revert InsufficientBalance(balance, amount);. This approach stores the error selector and the typed arguments, which is far smaller on-chain than a string message. Use custom errors when you want to report values back to the caller while minimizing gas. They also make it easier for frontends and block explorers to decode failure reasons without parsing strings. A practical pattern is to define a set of domain-specific errors at the top of your contract and use them consistently across functions. Remember not to hide sensitive internal state in error arguments; error data is visible in transaction traces. A common misconception is that custom errors are only about readability; their primary advantage is gas savings because strings are dynamic and more expensive to encode. In the Wallet example you will see InsufficientFunds(balance, amount) used to report available and requested quantities. When refactoring a string revert into a custom error, measure gas with a profiler to confirm the improvement. A closing question: which frequent revert messages in your codebase could be converted to typed errors for both clarity and cost reduction?

Solidity has three primary data locations you will use frequently: storage, memory, and calldata. storage persists on-chain and is the most expensive to write; every SSTORE and SLOAD has a real gas cost. Use storage only for true persistent state. memory is temporary and exists for the scope of a function call; it is cheaper than storage and useful for local copies and return buffers. calldata is immutable data provided by external function calls. For external functions that accept large arrays or byte buffers but do not modify them, calldata is the cheapest and avoids copying into memory. A common rule: for external function parameters that you will not mutate, declare them as calldata to avoid needless copying. For example, a function that accepts bytes calldata data returns data. length without copying it into memory. Also note that reading from storage inside tight loops is costly; prefer copying a storage reference into memory when you will access it multiple times in a function. A common misconception is that memory is free—it is not, but it is substantially cheaper than storage for temporary operations. Always ask: does this value need to be stored across transactions? If yes, use storage. If the value is transient or an external input that won’t be modified, favor memory or calldata respectively to reduce gas.

Storage writes are the single most expensive operations you will perform on-chain. Designing your contract to minimize SSTORE calls reduces deployment and per-call costs. Start by asking whether a value truly needs to persist. If it is only necessary for off-chain UIs or analytics, emit an event instead of writing to storage. Events are significantly cheaper than SSTORE and enable efficient retrieval by indexers. When you must update storage, try to batch updates or avoid toggling a storage slot repeatedly. Another pattern is to keep frequently changing counters in smaller packed slots or update derived values off-chain. Also be mindful of initializations: writing a zero to a slot that was already zero still consumes gas, so set defaults carefully. Best practice includes copying storage into memory for multiple reads inside a function and writing back only once if needed. For loops that update storage, consider accumulating results in memory and performing a single storage write at the end. A common mistake is treating events as ephemeral and storing the same data anyway. If the contract doesn't need to read the data on-chain later, prefer events for logging actions like deposits or user actions. Finally, marking read-only helpers view or pure allows callers to simulate behavior off-chain without a transaction cost.

Loops can be attractive but expensive when they repeatedly access storage or iterate over unbounded arrays. A loop that touches storage on every iteration multiplies SLOAD and SSTORE costs. Prefer designs that keep arrays small and bounded, or offload full scans to off-chain indexers. For on-chain processing, use pagination patterns so each transaction does a limited chunk of work. When iterating, copy frequently used storage values into memory once and reuse the in-memory copy to avoid multiple SLOADs. Short-circuiting with logical operators is another inexpensive gas control: expressions using && and || evaluate left to right and stop as soon as the outcome is determined. For example, require(condition1 && expensiveCheck(), "Error") will avoid calling expensiveCheck when condition1 is false. A common mistake is writing require with multiple expensive calls that always run; instead, reorder conditions so cheap checks run first. Also be careful with unbounded for loops across user-controlled collections. Concrete pattern: if you need to remove multiple elements, consider a mapping-based approach or mark items inactive and prune off-chain. The core rule: bound work performed in a single transaction and favor memory copies and short-circuit ordering to minimize repeated or unnecessary gas usage.

Solidity packs state variables into 256-bit storage slots where possible. By grouping smaller variables such as uint8, uint64, and bool together, you can place multiple values in a single slot and reduce the number of SSTORE operations required. The lesson provides a concrete struct example: UserData with uint256 id; uint128 lastLogin; bool isAdmin; uint64 reputation; initially this layout typically uses multiple slots because of the large uint256. Reordering fields so the smaller ones are grouped together and the large uint256 sits separately helps the compiler pack them more efficiently. For instance, placing uint64 reputation, uint128 lastLogin, bool isAdmin together allows them to fit within a single 256-bit slot, and keeping uint256 id in its own slot. A common misconception is that ordering doesn't matter; in practice the compiler packs contiguous smaller fields into the same slot if their combined width fits within 256 bits. When optimizing, weigh readability and future changes against packing gains: adding another large variable may break a packing strategy and increase slots. Always test with the compiler and examine the storage layout to confirm the expected packing. The payoff comes when writing or updating these fields: fewer slots mean fewer SSTOREs and lower gas for state changes.

Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, require and revert are for external checks and refund remaining gas, while assert signals internal invariants and consumes remaining gas. Second, custom errors are the preferred production pattern to report typed failure data while saving gas compared to string messages. Third, choose data locations deliberately: storage is persistent and expensive, memory is temporary for call-time work, and calldata is the cheapest for immutable external inputs. Each of these choices impacts safety, clarity, and transaction cost. Keep these principles in mind when writing or auditing contracts: match error primitives to failure types, prefer custom errors for frequent or data-rich reverts, and minimize persistent writes. These core rules will guide you to safer and more economical smart contracts. Here are the practical patterns you can use right away. First, minimize storage writes: batch updates, avoid toggling slots unnecessarily, and favor events for off-chain logs. Second, use calldata for external arguments that won't be modified and memory for local repeated reads. Third, pack small state variables to reduce the number of storage slots, reordering struct fields when safe. Fourth, bound loops and prefer pagination, copying storage into memory for heavy reads and ordering boolean checks to short-circuit expensive operations. Together these practices lower gas for both deployment and daily interactions, improving UX and adoption. The best approach is iterative: apply one optimization, measure with a gas profiler, and keep the change only when it yields a real improvement without compromising correctness or maintainability.
